title: Intrinsic Noise & Noise Figure
description: Thermal, shot and 1/f noise, noise bandwidth, noise figure and the Vn–In model for low-noise amplifier design.

study.title: Thermal (Johnson) noise
study.body: Every resistance produces a random open-circuit noise voltage from the thermal motion of its electrons, whatever it is made of. Model it as a noiseless resistor with a series source $V_t$ (Thévenin) or a parallel current source $I_t = \sqrt{4kTB/R}$ (Norton). This unit uses $k = 1.38\times10^{-23}$ J/K and $T$ = 290 K, so $4kT = 1.6\times10^{-20}$ W/Hz: 1 kΩ gives **4 nV/√Hz**. The noise grows with $\sqrt{R}$ and $\sqrt{B}$.

study.title: What makes noise, and what doesn't
study.body: Only elements that dissipate energy produce thermal noise: an ideal L or C is noiseless. The thermal noise of any passive network equals that of a resistor $\mathrm{Re}\{Z\}$, so two resistors in parallel are as noisy as $R_1 \parallel R_2$. The **available noise power** (delivered into a matched load) is $kTB$, independent of $R$: $4\times10^{-21}$ W per hertz, i.e. **−174 dBm/Hz**.

study.title: Equivalent noise bandwidth
study.body: $B$ is the width of an ideal brick-wall filter that passes the same noise power as the real response $|A(f)|^2$. A single-pole low-pass has $B = \frac{\pi}{2}f_{3dB} \approx 1.57 f_{3dB}$; two poles 1.22, three 1.15, and for many poles $B \approx f_{3dB}$. For an RC low-pass this gives $B = 1/(4RC)$, so its output noise is $\sqrt{kT/C}$, independent of $R$.

study.title: Shot, contact (1/f) and popcorn noise
study.body:
- **Shot noise**: a DC current crossing a potential barrier (a pn junction) consists of individual charges; white, with $q = 1.6\times10^{-19}$ C.
- **Contact (flicker, 1/f) noise**: fluctuating conductivity of imperfect contacts, carbon resistors and semiconductors; proportional to $I_{dc}$, power density $\propto 1/f$ (equal power per decade), so it dominates at low frequencies.
- **Popcorn (burst) noise**: random steps in the output caused by a junction defect; a manufacturing problem, worst in high-impedance circuits.

study.title: Adding and measuring noise
study.body: Uncorrelated noise sources add as powers: take the root of the sum of squares (RSS). Fully correlated sources would add linearly. Thermal noise is Gaussian, so its peak value is unbounded; peaks exceeding $4V_{rms}$ occur only 0.006 % of the time, so a **crest factor of 4** is used. On an oscilloscope, $V_{rms} \approx V_{pp}/8$ (ignore the odd extreme peak); a true-rms meter needs a bandwidth of at least 10× the noise bandwidth.

study.title: Noise factor, noise figure, noise temperature
study.body: The **noise factor** $F$ compares an amplifier with a noiseless one fed by the same resistive source $R_s$ at 290 K; $F = 1$ is perfect; the noise figure is $NF = 10\log_{10}F$ dB. Equivalent: total input noise $V_{nt} = \sqrt{4kTBR_sF}$, or a source heated by $T_e$. $F$ depends on $R_s$, so compare figures only at the same $R_s$. For cascaded stages (Friis) $F = F_1 + \frac{F_2-1}{G_1} + \frac{F_3-1}{G_1G_2} + \dots$ (power gains): a high-gain first stage sets the noise.

study.title: The $V_n$–$I_n$ amplifier model
study.body: Any amplifier's noise can be modelled by a voltage source $v_n$ and a current source $i_n$ at a noiseless input (densities in V/√Hz and A/√Hz; multiply by $\sqrt B$ for rms). $i_n$ flows through $R_s$, so $v_n$ dominates at low $R_s$ and $i_nR_s$ at high $R_s$. $R_{opt} = v_n/i_n$ gives the **lowest noise factor**, $F_{min} = 1 + v_ni_n/(2kT)$, but the lowest total noise is always at the lowest $R_s$. Bipolar inputs: low $v_n$ (low-$R_s$ sources); JFET inputs: tiny $i_n$ (high-$R_s$ sources); op amps are noisier than a discrete stage (two input transistors, ≈ √2 more).

steps.title: Thermal noise
steps.body: Any resistor at temperature $T$ generates a random rms voltage $V_t$ across its open terminals, even with no current flowing. $B$ is the noise bandwidth of the system that observes it. With $k = 1.38\times10^{-23}$ J/K and $T$ = 290 K, $4kT = 1.6\times10^{-20}$ W/Hz.

steps.prompt: Find the rms thermal noise voltage of a {{R|Ω}} resistor observed in a noise bandwidth of {{B|Hz}} (T = 290 K).
A 100 nF capacitor placed in parallel with a 10 kΩ resistor adds its own thermal noise voltage to the circuit.
steps.explanation: An ideal capacitor cannot dissipate energy, so it cannot generate thermal noise. It only **shapes** the resistor's noise: the RC limits the noise bandwidth. In general the noise of a passive network equals the thermal noise of $\mathrm{Re}\{Z\}$.

steps.title: Noise bandwidth
steps.body: Real filters roll off gradually, so noise beyond $f_{3dB}$ still gets through. The **equivalent noise bandwidth** $B$ is the width of an ideal filter with the same area under $|A|^2$. For a single pole it is $\frac{\pi}{2}f_{3dB}$; for three or more poles $B \approx f_{3dB}$.

steps.prompt: A resistor $R$ = {{R|Ω}} is shunted by $C$ = {{C|F}} (an RC low-pass at T = 290 K).

ask.prompt: Find the equivalent noise bandwidth $B$.
Find the total rms noise voltage across the capacitor.
ask.explanation: $B = \frac{\pi}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2\pi RC} = \frac{1}{4RC}$ = {{Bn|Hz}}, so $V = \sqrt{4kTR\cdot\frac{1}{4RC}} = \sqrt{kT/C}$ = √(4.0×10⁻²¹ / {{C|F}}) = **{{sqrt(4.002e-21/C)|V}}**. $R$ cancels: a larger $R$ is noisier but narrows the bandwidth by the same factor.

steps.title: Other intrinsic noise sources
steps.body:
- **Shot noise**: DC current crossing a junction is a stream of discrete charges, $I_{sh} = \sqrt{2qI_{dc}B}$ (white).
- **Contact or 1/f noise**: imperfect contacts and semiconductors; proportional to the DC current, power density $\propto 1/f$, so it rules at low frequencies.
- **Popcorn noise**: random steps caused by a junction defect; better manufacturing removes it.

steps.prompt: Match each noise type to its cause
pairs: DC current crossing a pn junction
Imperfect contacts; grows at low f
steps.explanation: Thermal noise needs only resistance and temperature. Shot noise needs current across a potential barrier. Contact noise needs current through an imperfect (non-homogeneous) conductor and has a 1/f power density. Popcorn noise comes from defects (often metallic impurities) in a junction.

steps.prompt: A diode carries a DC current of {{I|A}}. Find the rms shot noise current in a noise bandwidth of {{B|Hz}}.
steps.explanation: $I_{sh} = \sqrt{2qI_{dc}B}$ = √(2 × 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ × {{I|A}} × {{B|Hz}}) = **{{sqrt(2*1.6e-19*I*B)|A}}**. Because it depends only on $I_{dc}$, a diode makes a handy calibrated white-noise source.

steps.prompt: Two uncorrelated noise sources of {{V1|V}} and {{V2|V}} rms appear in series. What is the total rms noise?
steps.explanation: Uncorrelated noise adds as power: $V = \sqrt{V_1^2 + V_2^2}$ = √(({{V1|V}})² + ({{V2|V}})²) = **{{sqrt(V1^2+V2^2)|V}}**. Adding the rms values linearly ({{V1+V2|V}}) is only right for fully correlated sources.

steps.prompt: Two resistors at 290 K are connected in parallel between terminals a and b.

ask.prompt: Find the noise voltage density at the open terminals.
ask.explanation: The network is as noisy as one resistor $R_1 \parallel R_2$ = {{Rp|Ω}}: $\sqrt{4kTR}$ = √(1.6×10⁻²⁰ × {{Rp|Ω}}) = **{{sqrt(1.6008e-20*Rp)|V/√Hz}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the rms open-circuit noise voltage in a bandwidth of {{B|Hz}}.
Find the rms Norton noise current (terminals shorted) in a bandwidth of {{B|Hz}}.
ask.explanation: $I_t = \sqrt{4kTB/R}$ with $R = R_1\parallel R_2$ = {{Rp|Ω}}: √(1.6×10⁻²⁰ × {{B|Hz}} / {{Rp|Ω}}) = **{{sqrt(1.6008e-20*B/Rp)|A}}**. (Equivalently, the two Norton currents add in RSS.)

steps.prompt: Find the available thermal noise power $kTB$ (T = 290 K) in a bandwidth of {{B|Hz}}, in dBm.
An amplifier has a white input noise density of {{vn|V/√Hz}} and a single-pole response with $f_{3dB}$ = {{f3|Hz}}. Find the total rms input-referred noise.
steps.explanation: Noise bandwidth $B = 1.57 f_{3dB}$ = {{pi/2*f3|Hz}}. $V_n = v_n\sqrt B$ = {{vn|V/√Hz}} × √({{pi/2*f3|Hz}}) = **{{vn*sqrt(pi/2*f3)|V}}**. Using $f_{3dB}$ itself would underestimate it by 20 % ({{vn*sqrt(f3)|V}}).

steps.prompt: An oscilloscope on the output of an amplifier with voltage gain {{A}} shows random noise of about {{Vpp|V}} peak-to-peak (ignoring a few rare peaks). Estimate the equivalent rms input noise.
steps.explanation: With a crest factor of 4, $V_{rms} \approx V_{pp}/8$ = {{Vpp/8|V}} at the output. Divide by the gain: {{Vpp/8|V}} / {{A}} = **{{Vpp/(8*A)|V}}** at the input.

steps.prompt: A photodiode current $I_{dc}$ = {{Idc|A}} flows through the feedback resistor $R_f$ = {{Rf|Ω}} of a transimpedance amplifier (B = {{B|Hz}}, T = 290 K).

ask.prompt: Find the rms output noise voltage caused by the photodiode's shot noise.
Find the rms output noise voltage caused by the thermal noise of $R_f$.
Find the total rms output noise from these two sources.
ask.explanation: Shot: $\sqrt{2qI_{dc}B}\,R_f$ = {{Vsh|V}}; thermal: $\sqrt{4kTR_fB}$ = {{Vth|V}}. Uncorrelated, so RSS: **{{sqrt(Vsh^2+Vth^2)|V}}**. Shot noise dominates once $I_{dc}R_f > 2kT/q \approx$ 50 mV.

steps.prompt: A sensor with $R_s$ = {{R|Ω}} delivers an rms signal of {{Vs|V}}. Only its own thermal noise matters, in a noise bandwidth of {{B|Hz}}. Find the signal-to-noise ratio in dB.
Set the noise bandwidth so that the {{R|Ω}} resistor produces {{Vtar|V}} rms of thermal noise.
steps.explanation: Solve $V_t = \sqrt{4kTRB}$ for $B$: $B = \frac{V_t^2}{4kTR}$ = ({{Vtar|V}})² / (1.6×10⁻²⁰ × {{R|Ω}}) = **{{Bt|Hz}}**. On the log–log plot the curve is a straight line with slope ½.

steps.title: Three ways to state amplifier noise
steps.body:
- Noise factor $F$ (or figure $NF = 10\log F$), always for a stated $R_s$.
- Noise temperature $T_e = 290(F-1)$: handy for very low-noise (radio) amplifiers.
- Noise sources $v_n$ and $i_n$: work for any source impedance; op-amp and FET data sheets use these.

steps.prompt: An amplifier has a noise figure of {{NF}} dB.

ask.prompt: Find its noise factor $F$.
Find its equivalent input noise temperature $T_e$ in kelvin.

steps.prompt: A {{Vs|V}} rms signal from a {{Rs|Ω}} source drives an amplifier with NF = {{NF}} dB (measured at this $R_s$). The noise bandwidth is {{B|Hz}}. Find the output signal-to-noise ratio in dB.
steps.explanation: Source noise $V_t = \sqrt{4kTR_sB}$ = {{Vt|V}}, so $(S/N)_{in}$ = 20 log({{Vs|V}} / {{Vt|V}}) = {{SNi||3}} dB. The amplifier degrades this by its noise figure: {{SNi||3}} − {{NF}} = **{{SNi-NF||3}} dB**.

steps.prompt: An amplifier with $v_n$ = {{vn|V/√Hz}} and $i_n$ = {{In*1e12||2}} pA/√Hz is driven from $R_s$ = {{Rs|Ω}} (T = 290 K).

ask.prompt: Find the total equivalent input noise density.
Find the total rms equivalent input noise in a {{B|Hz}} noise bandwidth.
Find the source resistance that gives the minimum noise factor.
Find the noise figure at this source resistance.

steps.prompt: An amplifier with $v_n$ = {{vn|V/√Hz}} and $i_n$ = {{In*1e12||2}} pA/√Hz is driven from $R_s$ = {{Rs|Ω}}. Which contribution dominates the total input noise?
steps.explanation: Compare the three densities: $\sqrt{4kTR_s}$ = {{t*1e9||2}} nV/√Hz, $v_n$ = {{vn*1e9||2}} nV/√Hz, $i_nR_s$ = {{c*1e9||2}} nV/√Hz. The largest dominates because they add in RSS. Low $R_s$ favours $v_n$, high $R_s$ favours $i_nR_s$.

steps.prompt: A preamplifier (NF = {{NF1}} dB, power gain {{G1}} dB) drives a second stage with NF = {{NF2}} dB. Find the overall noise figure.
Which input stage gives the lowest noise for a piezo sensor with a 1 MΩ source resistance?
options: Any op amp, with a series resistor to match $R_{opt}$
steps.explanation: At 1 MΩ the term $i_nR_s$ dominates: a bipolar input with $i_n$ = 1 pA/√Hz gives 1 µV/√Hz, far above the source's own 0.13 µV/√Hz. A JFET's gate leakage gives $i_n$ in the fA/√Hz range. Adding resistance never helps.

steps.prompt: If the source resistance is below $R_{opt} = v_n/i_n$, adding a series resistor to bring it up to $R_{opt}$ improves the signal-to-noise ratio.
steps.explanation: The noise factor drops, but the total noise rises: the extra resistor adds its own thermal noise and more $i_nR$ noise while the signal stays the same. Minimum $F$ is not maximum S/N. Only a (nearly lossless) **transformer** can raise the source resistance seen by the amplifier and improve S/N.

steps.prompt: A strain-gauge bridge ($R_s$ = {{Rs|Ω}}) delivers {{Vs|V}} rms to a preamplifier with $v_n$ = {{vn|V/√Hz}} and $i_n$ = {{In*1e12||2}} pA/√Hz. The noise bandwidth is {{B|Hz}} (T = 290 K).

ask.prompt: Find the total equivalent input noise voltage $V_{nt}$.
Find the output signal-to-noise ratio in dB.
By what factor must the bandwidth shrink to raise S/N by 6 dB (noise halved)?
ask.explanation: All terms scale with $\sqrt B$, so halving the noise voltage needs **4×** less bandwidth: $\sqrt{1/4} = 1/2$, i.e. +6 dB.

steps.prompt: A {{Rs|Ω}} source (e.g. a moving-coil pickup) drives an amplifier with $v_n$ = {{vn|V/√Hz}} and $i_n$ = {{In*1e12||2}} pA/√Hz. An ideal transformer may be inserted between them.

ask.prompt: Find the noise figure without a transformer.
ask.explanation: $F = 1 + \frac{v_n^2 + i_n^2R_s^2}{4kTR_s}$ = {{Fw||3}}, so $NF$ = **{{10*log10(Fw)||3}} dB**. $v_n$ is large compared with the source's own {{sqrt(1.6008e-20*Rs)|V/√Hz}}.

ask.prompt: Find the turns ratio $n = N_2/N_1$ that transforms $R_s$ to $R_{opt}$.
ask.explanation: $R_{opt} = v_n/i_n$ = {{Ro|Ω}}. The transformer multiplies the source resistance by $n^2$: $n = \sqrt{R_{opt}/R_s}$ = √({{Ro|Ω}} / {{Rs|Ω}}) = **{{sqrt(Ro/Rs)||3}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the signal-to-noise improvement (in dB) obtained with that transformer.
ask.explanation: With the transformer $F = F_{min} = 1 + \frac{v_ni_n}{2kT}$ = {{Fm||3}}. The source S/N is unchanged by an ideal transformer, so the improvement is $F_{without}/F_{with}$ = {{Fw||3}}/{{Fm||3}}, i.e. **{{10*log10(Fw/Fm)||3}} dB** (ignoring winding resistance).

steps.prompt: An antenna feeds a receiver (NF = {{NF3}} dB) through a matched cable with {{Lc}} dB loss. A low-noise amplifier (NF = {{NF1}} dB, gain {{G1}} dB) is added. A matched lossy cable has $F = L$ and $G = 1/L$.

ask.prompt: Find the system noise figure with the LNA mounted **at the antenna** (before the cable).
Find the system noise figure with the LNA at the **receiver end** (after the cable).
ask.explanation: Now the cable is first: $F = L + \frac{F_1-1}{1/L} + \frac{F_3-1}{G_1/L} = L F_1 + \frac{(F_3-1)L}{G_1}$ = {{L*F1||3}} + {{(F3-1)*L/g||3}} = {{Fb||3}} → **{{10*log10(Fb)||3}} dB**. The cable loss adds directly to the noise figure, so put the LNA at the antenna.

steps.prompt: A receiver has a noise bandwidth of {{B|Hz}} and NF = {{NF}} dB. The demodulator needs S/N = {{SNR}} dB.

ask.prompt: Find the minimum input signal power (sensitivity) in dBm.
ask.explanation: Noise floor: −174 dBm/Hz + 10 log B ({{10*log10(B)||3}} dB) + NF ({{NF}} dB) = {{P-SNR||4}} dBm. Add the required S/N: **{{P||4}} dBm**.

ask.prompt: Express that sensitivity as an rms voltage across the 50 Ω input.
ask.explanation: Convert to watts: $P = 10^{(P_{dBm}-30)/10}$ W with $P_{dBm}$ = {{P||4}}. Then $V = \sqrt{PR}$ = $\sqrt{50\,\Omega \cdot P}$ = **{{sqrt(50*10^((P-30)/10))|V}}**.

steps.prompt: To measure noise factor, a shot-noise diode is placed across the amplifier input with $R_s$ = {{Rs|Ω}}. The output noise power doubles (+3 dB) at a diode current of {{Idc|A}}. Find the noise figure.
steps.explanation: Doubling the output power means the diode's noise $I_{sh}R_s$ equals all the existing input noise, $\sqrt{4kTBR_sF}$. So $2qI_{dc}BR_s^2 = 4kTBR_sF$ and $F = \frac{2q}{4kT}I_{dc}R_s = 20\,I_{dc}R_s$ (at 290 K) = 20 × {{Idc|A}} × {{Rs|Ω}} = {{20*Idc*Rs||3}}, i.e. **{{10*log10(20*Idc*Rs)||3}} dB**. Neither the gain nor $B$ needs to be known.
